changes.before: A separate project reports that an external library type cannot be found. You add only using Vendor.Tools;. What has that change actually done?
changes.after: Know when a library needs a package reference and when it is already available.

before: NuGet packages can supply libraries and other build assets. A PackageReference in the project records a package identity and version; using only imports a namespace.

In .NET 10, dotnet package add PACKAGE --version VERSION --project App.csproj adds a reference and normally restores it. PACKAGE and VERSION are placeholders: select a real reviewed package and compatible version rather than running the placeholder command.

Restore resolves and downloads dependencies; it does not prove the library behaves correctly. Check publisher, license, compatibility and security advisories before adding a dependency. The companion deliberately uses only built-in .NET libraries.
Commit the project’s intended dependency configuration and review version changes. Do not upgrade an unrelated package merely to silence a compiler error.
Expected behavior from this example: ["read","test"]. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer: Inspect a disposable project file before and after adding a reviewed package. Identify the reference, then restore and build; do not use an unknown package just for this exercise. This is a separate local practice task, not a requirement to mark the reading complete.
after: A dependency is code your project relies on. NuGet packages can supply libraries and build files. Some libraries are already included with your target .NET version.

A PackageReference in the project file names a package and version. In .NET 10, dotnet package add PACKAGE --version VERSION --project App.csproj adds one. PACKAGE and VERSION are placeholders for a chosen real package and version.

Restore finds and downloads the required dependencies. It does not test whether they behave correctly. Review the publisher, license, compatibility, and known security issues before choosing a package.
System.Text.Json is already available to this .NET 10 console project. The example needs no extra package installation.
The program prints ["read","test"]. JsonSerializer turns the array into JSON text.

using makes namespace members easier to name; it does not add a missing library. Keep intended dependency versions in the project configuration and review changes rather than upgrading unrelated packages to hide an error.

before.question: A separate project reports that an external library type cannot be found. You add only using Vendor.Tools;. What has that change actually done?
choices: Installed and trusted the vendor package
Requested shorter names from a namespace, without adding the missing dependency
Proved the package version is compatible
before.explanation: A using directive does not change project references. Confirm the intended dependency and add the appropriate project or package reference.

after.question: An external library is missing. You add only using Vendor.Tools;. What does that do?
choices: Allows shorter names if the namespace is available, but adds no dependency
Proves a package version is compatible
after.explanation: A using directive only affects naming. The intended library still needs an appropriate package or project reference.
